questions.question: What property makes Z/pZ a field when p is prime?
options: Every nonzero residue has an inverse
Every residue has additive order p
Every product avoids modular wrap
Every integer becomes a generator
questions.explanation: When p is prime, each nonzero residue is coprime to p. Extended Euclid gives a multiplicative inverse for every such residue.

questions.question: Why should a field element carry its modulus?
options: It prevents mixing values from different fields
It avoids reducing after multiplication steps
It makes composite moduli behave like primes
It replaces inverses with ordinary division
questions.explanation: The same integer value can mean different elements in different fields. Carrying p lets code reject accidental cross-field arithmetic.

questions.question: What is the inverse of 5 in F_17?
options: 7, since 5 times 7 equals 1 mod 17
5, since every element is its own inverse
12, since negative five wraps in F_17
0, since inverses vanish after reduction
questions.explanation: 5 * 7 = 35, and 35 mod 17 is 1. Therefore 7 is the multiplicative inverse of 5 in F_17.

questions.question: What happens when code treats Z/15Z as GF(15)?
options: Nonzero values may multiply to zero
Addition stops being closed in the set
The residue zero gains many inverses
Every denominator becomes invertible
questions.explanation: In Z/15Z, 3 and 5 are nonzero but 3 * 5 = 0 mod 15. That zero-divisor behavior means the ring is not a field.

questions.question: In F_p, what does the multiplicative order of a nonzero element measure?
options: The first k where a to the k equals 1
The count of additions needed to reach p
The largest residue produced by powers of a
The number of primes smaller than p
questions.explanation: The multiplicative order of a is the smallest positive k with a^k = 1 in the field. Generators have order p - 1.

questions.question: Why must Lagrange interpolation use distinct x-coordinates modulo p?
options: Repeated x values create zero denominators
Repeated x values remove all coefficients
Repeated x values force p to be composite
Repeated x values change addition rules
questions.explanation: Lagrange basis terms divide by x_i - x_j. If two x-coordinates are equal modulo p, that denominator is zero and cannot be inverted.

questions.question: What does it mean for g to be a generator of F_p^*?
options: Its powers list every nonzero element
Its additions list every field element
Its inverse is always equal to itself
Its value is larger than all residues
questions.explanation: A generator has multiplicative order p - 1. Its powers enumerate the entire nonzero multiplicative group.

questions.question: What is the safer engineering habit for GF(p) code?
options: Validate p, normalize values, reject zero division
Accept any modulus, normalize values, skip inverses
Validate p, skip reduction, allow mixed moduli
Accept any modulus, allow division by residues
questions.explanation: Prime-field code should verify the modulus, keep values canonical, and reject impossible divisions. Those checks prevent composite-modulus and mixed-field bugs.
